[QUERENT] shelf-order hermeneutics

[ANSWER]

Shelf-order hermeneutics is the study of how the physical arrangement, proximity, and sequencing of books on a shelf communicate implicit meaning, shape canonical formation, and guide interpretation. [1, 2]
Core Concepts

* Implicit Argument: A bookshelf silently asserts what belongs together, what comes first or has priority, and what is treated as peripheral or marginal without ever stating it directly. [1]
* Material Hermeneutics: It shifts interpretation away from purely textual analysis to include the physical, spatial, and archival conditions of how a collection is assembled and displayed. [1]
* Canonical Shaping: Grouping or ordering works (such as in libraries using the Library of Congress Classes & Shelving system) forces readers to encounter texts through an institutional or curated narrative. [1]

Would you like to explore how shelf-order hermeneutics applies to a specific library classification system, or look into the theoretical paper by Lee Sharks on the material argument of collections?
